topic: Qualcomm unveils HBC near-memory AI architecture
headline_marked: [[Qualcomm reveals HBC near-memory AI architecture]] with AI250/AI350 accelerators, touting 6x HBM bandwidth-per-watt
headline: Qualcomm reveals HBC near-memory AI architecture with AI250/AI350 accelerators, touting 6x HBM bandwidth-per-watt
summary: Qualcomm's new HBC architecture promises 6x higher bandwidth-per-watt than HBM and 200x capacity over on-chip SRAM, aiming to break the AI memory wall.
details: Qualcomm has introduced its High-Bandwidth Compute (HBC) near-memory architecture, designed to overcome the 'memory wall' that limits AI workload performance. The company claims HBC offers 6x higher bandwidth-per-watt compared to HBM and over 200x capacity compared to on-chip SRAM.

HBC disaggregates the AI accelerator from the system-on-chip (SoC) and places it directly under the LPDDR DRAM stack. This connection uses through-silicon vias, providing maximum bandwidth and capacity without requiring expensive HBM memory or advanced packaging.

According to Tony Pialis, EVP and GM of Data Center Business at Qualcomm, this approach delivers performance advantages similar to SRAM with the density of stacked memory. It aims to reduce power consumption, heat, and eliminate the costly silicon interposer used in HBM solutions.

While near-memory compute architectures have been explored by DRAM makers before, Qualcomm's implementation aims for broader adoption. Other companies, like GUC with its DRAM-on-Logic (DoL) technology, have also proposed similar solutions to achieve high memory bandwidth.

Qualcomm has not yet disclosed the actual performance numbers for HBC, nor the precise function of the HBC accelerator itself. This makes direct comparisons to other near-memory solutions, such as GUC's offering, challenging at this stage.

The company also outlined its HBC roadmap, featuring future accelerators. The AI200 will use LPDDR5X, while its successors, the AI250 and AI300, will leverage 1st and 2nd Generation HBC, promising 18X and 54X the bandwidth of the AI200, respectively.

topic: Cellebrite tools used by Russia despite cutoff
headline_marked: [[Russian authorities used Cellebrite tools]] to hack opponent's phone after company cut ties
headline: Russian authorities used Cellebrite tools to hack opponent's phone after company cut ties
summary: A new report reveals Russian government agencies used Cellebrite's phone hacking tools on a political opponent, despite the forensics firm claiming it had ceased all sales and services to Russia months prior.
details: Russian authorities reportedly used phone hacking technology from forensics firm Cellebrite to access a political opponent's device while he was in custody. This occurred despite Cellebrite's public announcement months earlier that it had cut all ties with Russian government agencies.

Cellebrite, an Israeli company with a U.S. headquarters, had stated in March 2021 it would "immediately" stop providing hardware and software to Russia. The company claims it can stop devices from functioning or receiving updates after terminating licenses.

However, researchers at The Citizen Lab found evidence that a Russian investigative unit used a Cellebrite tool to break into the iPhone of opposition politician Andrey Pivovarov in June 2021. This was three months after Cellebrite's announced withdrawal.

The incident raises questions about the true control Western tech companies have over their tools once they are "in the wild." It suggests that even with terminated licenses, powerful surveillance technologies can continue to be abused by former customers.

Human rights lawyers argue that simply ceasing sales or revoking licenses is insufficient if companies don't demand dismantling of tools or implement remote disabling capabilities. They also highlight the lack of transparency regarding customer accountability.

Cellebrite's Chief Marketing Officer stated to The Citizen Lab that all sales and services to the Russian Federation were terminated in March 2021, and any subsequent use of legacy hardware is "entirely unauthorized." The company did not respond to specific follow-up questions from TechCrunch.
